newsitem.title: USA: NYC expects Washington to sue it over Croton water.
newsitem.headline: NYC expects Washington to sue it over Croton water.

text.p: New York City expects the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) to file a suit as soon as this week to make the city speed building a controversial plant to clean part of its water system, city officials said Tuesday.

New York City was supposed to start up a costly, new filtration plant for the Croton system, located in Westchester County, which is just north of the city, by the end of 1999, explained Patrick McCoy, a spokesman for the city Municipal Water Finance Authority.

But that deadline has been missed, and while the federal Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) will go along with an extension, city officials said Washington does not want to let the Giuliani Administration push the deadline back to 2007.
So the federal environmental regulators have turned to the DOJ to force the city to build the plant more swiftly.

The potential lawsuit was disclosed in the preliminary official statement (POS) for an upcoming $635 million bond sale by the Municipal Water Finance Authority slated for the week of April 28 and through an underwriting syndicate headed by J.P. Morgan Securities Inc.

"What the DOJ has said is that they're amenable to changing the agreement and they want to have it in an order that is enforceable in a federal court and we've agreed to do it that way," said Elizabeth St. Clair, chief of the environmental law division, city Office of the Corporation Counsel. She was referring to a 1992 pact between the city and the state that sets a timetable for a new filtration plant.
"At some point later this week, they are probably going to file a complaint and we will continue negotiating with them," she added.

The Giuliani Administration is studying the need for filtering Croton's water system, which provides New York City with about 10 percent of its water, and possible locations for a new treatment plant, a thorny issue.
The cost of the new plant has increased substantially while the city has grappled with the issue, rising to $828 million from $549 million, according to the water authority POS.
The EPA has not completely ruled out delaying the new plant's start until 2007.

Mary Mears, a spokeswoman for the regional office, said, "We've not said No or Yes to a date. We've told them we're willing to consider dates as long as they are the most reasonable dates they can have the plant built."
She explained the EPA hopes to file a settlement at the same time as it files its case in court. This will let it get a court-imposed order that can be backed with penalites.
The city provides nine million people of people who live in the city and five nearby counties with 1.1 billion gallons of water a day.

None of the water now is filtered, and plans to build a treatment plant for the Croton system are separate from a pact the city, state and upstate communities reached to protect the watershed around 19 reservoirs without building a billion-dollar filter system or stifling development.
Around 700,000 people live around the Croton watershed, which could cause problems with run-off, the spokesman for the municipal water authority said.
The city disinfects the water, but the EPA says that will not be sufficient in the future, given the number of sewage treatment plants in the area.

Surface water systems like Croton are more likely to be contaminated and spread diseases than ground water systems. So Washington gave localities throughout the nation until the end of 1991 to prove that their systems did not need filtering.
One of the main reasons for the delay in the Giuliani Administration's plans for a new filtration plant for Croton is the battle over where it should be built.

City officials, who declined to be named, speculated Republican Mayor Rudolph Giuliani might benefit from having a court set a deadline as this would ease some of the pressure on him during an election year.
A spokesman for the mayor was not immediately available.
Two potential sites in the Bronx, which a Croton aqueduct runs through, are strenuously opposed by local officials.
The Jerome Park Reservoir has about 50,000 residents, and is one of the borough's most stable communities, according to an official who works for the Bronx Borough President.
Another possible site, Van Cortlandt Park, also was rejected by a spokesman for the Bronx Borough President, who hopes to win the Democratic primary and run for mayor.
"Oh, no, no site in the Bronx. They should take it up to Westchester County, where it belongs," said J.J. Gonzalez, a spokesman for the Bronx Borough President, Fernando Ferrer.
((--U.S. Municipal Desk, 212-859-1650))
